Country-level: The most distinctive cue is the bright yellow zebra-style crosswalk across the carriageway. In Europe, yellow crosswalks are strongly associated with Switzerland, whereas most neighboring countries use white. Roadway edge and center markings appear white and yellow in a combination typical for Swiss urban streets, where yellow is also used for reserved/bus lanes and emphasis at crossings. Architecture (mid-rise stucco apartment blocks with balconies), right-hand traffic, EU-style vehicles, and mountainous hillside in the distance are consistent with Switzerland. Overhead catenary/utility lines over the roadway indicate a tram or trolleybus corridor, common in major Swiss cities.
City-level: Among Swiss cities with extensive street-running tram/trolleybus wiring and broad urban corridors—Zurich, Basel, Bern, Geneva, Lausanne—the scene best matches Zurich/Lausanne/Geneva architectural vibe, but the combination of a wide multi-lane street, central-European block style, and a green hill backdrop closely fits Zurich, where many streets run toward the Uetliberg/Zürichberg hills. Basel is flatter and often shows Rhine-related cues; Bern’s old town has sandstone arcades; Geneva often shows Lake/Leman cues and French signage which are absent here. Thus Zurich is the most plausible.
Street-level: The specific street shows a long yellow crosswalk spanning multiple lanes, yellow dashed bus/turn lane markings at the right edge, curb-separated sidewalk with short gray bollards with red tops, and overhead suspended street lamps and tram/trolley wires aligned along a gentle uphill corridor toward a wooded hill. This combination—tram wiring, wide carriageway, and pronounced yellow markings—suggests an inner-district Zurich arterial rather than a small residential street.
